item.title: Tour: Curators’ Tour of "Continental Shift" and "Care and Concern" — Fri Sep 18, 1:00 PM — Ackland Art Museum
item.description:

In this tour, the curators of both Continental Shift: Recent Acquisitions of African Art and Care and Concern: Recent Acquisitions of Modern and Contemporary Art discuss the ways that the recently-acquired works of art exhibited affect the Museum’s collection of African and contemporary art. Students who attend can scan the QR code provided at the event to receive CLE credit.

item.title: Palmer Presents: Salon Conversations with Dr. Worth K. Hayes — Fri Sep 18, 6:00 PM — Charlotte Hawkins Brown Museum
item.description:
Join the Charlotte Hawkins Brown Museum and Dr. Worth Hayes virtually as we explore the life and work of Doris Allen Anderson, founder and leader of the Howalton Day School in Chicago, IL. This school and its progressive curriculum was a haven for Chicago's Black community from 1946 to 1999. Dr. Worth K. Hayes, author of Schools of Our Own: Chicago’s Golden Age of Black Private Education and a coming biography of Doris Allen Anderson, will lead this conversation. We are excited to host you in our salon!
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: Wild Mushroom Hike — Fri Sep 18, 6:00 PM — Lake James State Park - Paddy's Creek Access
item.description:
Ever been curious about mushrooms, those weird and wild organisms that unexpectedly pop out of the ground? This program is for you! This short, moderate hike will introduce participants to the fungus family, and everyone will have a chance to find living specimens and examine them closely.
Attendees are welcome to bring in samples of mushrooms from their own property. Place any samples in a paper bag, and do not eat any mushrooms found, as they may be poisonous.
The hike will begin from the Linville Gorge Overlook parking lot, which is just inside the Paddy's Creek Access's entrance gate on the right.
Please note: collecting mushrooms is prohibited in North Carolina State Parks. There will be no foray as part of this program.
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: Luminary & Freedom Stories — Fri Sep 18, 7:00 PM — Bennett Place State Historic Site
item.description:
During this special luminary program, Bennett Place invites you to reflect on the end of the Civil War as a momentous step towards freedom for all Americans and the end of chattel slavery in the United States.
Walk among 3,310 luminaries - one for every 1,000 enslaved people in North Carolina - and reflect on experiences of enslavement and freedom. Historians dot the path and share stories of people's pathways to freedom and life after slavery & the Civil War.
---
Harriet Ann Daves recalled just how monumental Civil War surrenders were for her family: "When the surrender came my grandfather came to my mother and told her: 'Well, you are as free as I am.'"
Claiming freedom was not so straightforward for the 331,059 enslaved women, children, and men in North Carolina during the Civil War. item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Sat Sep 19 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

item.title: Spy Training 101: Decode a Secret Message — Sat Sep 19 — North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences
item.description:
Pretend you’ve been recruited as a member of the Culper Spy Ring, and you need to know how to decipher a message written in invisible ink. Supplies include a paint brush, water, drying cloth, vitriol (diluted sulfuric acid), Thomas Jefferson cipher and “furnace box.” Read the clues to find the coin with a hidden message, reveal the message using the brush and vitriol, then use the cipher to decode the message.
Contact: Nancy Locquet Absillis, nancy.locquet@naturalsciences.org
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words — Sat Sep 19 — Welborn Gallery
item.description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026
This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.
An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.
Refreshments will be served.
Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

The event will begin with a talk from a Lake James State Park Ranger about local ecology before participants head into the field to explore diverse habitats and search for species. Whether you are an experienced naturalist or simply curious about the natural world, all skill levels are welcome. This is a great opportunity to learn more about the biodiversity of Lake James State Park while contributing valuable observations to our collective understanding of the park's natural resources.

item.title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence — Sat Sep 19, 10:00 AM — Kings Mountain Historical Museum
item.description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.
The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage — Sat Sep 19, 10:00 AM — Gregg Museum of Art & Design
item.description:
Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: Patch-a-Palooza at Vance Birthplace — Sat Sep 19, 10:00 AM — Governor Zebulon B. Vance Birthplace
item.description:
Join us on Saturday, September 19th for a day of sensory learning and fun at Vance Birthplace! Patch-a-Palooza welcomes families with K-8th grade children to try their hands at various historic activities from writing with a quill pen to playing historic games. Each learning station has a stamp, and children who earn a stamp from every station will receive a Vance Birthplace patch along with their take-home crafts. This is a great opportunity for children to learn about life in Western North Carolina in the 1800s while working on their fine motor, artistic, and critical thinking skills.
Admission is $7 per child to cover the cost of craft supplies. Adults may enter for free unless they choose to participate in the crafts. Enter through the visitor center to pay admission and receive stamp cards. This event is appropriate for all ages but is primarily geared toward elementary and middle grade learners.

item.title: Militia Muster Event - Experience 18th Century — Sat Sep 19, 11:00 AM — Hickory Ridge History Museum
item.description:
Experience life in the Southern Appalachian backcountry during the American Revolution at our Militia Muster! Guests of all ages are invited to step into the world of 18th-century militia life through interactive demonstrations, reenactments, and hands-on activities.
Watch as 18th Century Militia reenactors bring history to life through drills, camp life, and mock recruitment scenes. Explore the daily challenges faced by settlers and soldiers, and learn more about what it took to fight for independence in the mountains of North Carolina.
This is a family-friendly, immersive educational event perfect for history lovers, homeschool families, and curious visitors of all ages.
Please call 828-264-2120 for ticketing information.

item.description:

item.title: Duke Arts Presents: Salix Piano Trio — Sun Sep 20, 2:00 PM — Baldwin Auditorium
item.description:
Experience the "probing, fiercely intelligent playing" (The Washington Post) of the Salix Piano Trio. Named for the "graceful and poetic weeping willow," the ensemble explores the chemistry between the violin, cello, and piano.
Sample a range of musical wonders when the Salixes elicit 18th-century elegance in Mozart's Piano Trio No. 5 and the smoky, Romantic turbulence of Brahms's Piano Trio No. 1. Composer Frank Bridge adds a cafe sound to traditional dances, while Jennifer Higdon conjures lithe Impressionism in her trio movement "Pale Yellow." The centerpiece of the evening comes from the 16-year-old Dmitri Shostakovich, whose plucky trio runs between lyrical beauty and impudence.
The piano trio began as a house band, once gathered around the family harpsichord. Four hundred years on, this close-knit combination, now anchored by the piano, continues to captivate both players and audiences.

item.title: CEE Seminar - Biofilm Dispersion: Regulatory Mechanisms, Emergent Phenotypes, and Clinical Consequences — Mon Sep 21, 12:00 PM — None
item.description:
Biofilm dispersion is a regulated developmental transition that enables bacteria to exit surface‑attached communities and re‑enter a planktonic state. This seminar will examine the molecular circuitry that drives dispersion, with emphasis on the environmental cues, signaling pathways, and phosphodiesterase networks that coordinate matrix degradation and cell release. Emerging data reveal that dispersed cells represent a transcriptionally distinct physiological state. Their unique phenotype, including heightened susceptibility, increased motility, enhanced dissemination potential, immune evasion, and elevated virulence traits, will be discussed. These features have important clinical implications, positioning dispersed cells as key contributors to biofilm persistence, dissemination, and the establishment of secondary infections, while also highlighting dispersion as a therapeutically relevant intervention point for biofilm control.

item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Tue Sep 22 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

item.description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.
The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!

item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Wed Sep 23 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

item.title: Spy Training 101: Decode a Secret Message — Wed Sep 23 — North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences
item.description:
Pretend you’ve been recruited as a member of the Culper Spy Ring, and you need to know how to decipher a message written in invisible ink. Supplies include a paint brush, water, drying cloth, vitriol (diluted sulfuric acid), Thomas Jefferson cipher and “furnace box.” Read the clues to find the coin with a hidden message, reveal the message using the brush and vitriol, then use the cipher to decode the message.
Contact: Nancy Locquet Absillis, nancy.locquet@naturalsciences.org
Source: NC Cultural Resources
